question: Why might a designer choose a strict grid system over a completely free form layout for a piece of editorial design?
lookingFor: Understanding that structure serves the reader's comprehension and consistency, not just aesthetics, while knowing when to break it deliberately.

bullets: Explain that a grid gives a reader predictable places to find information, which speeds up reading across a whole publication
Note that consistency across many pages or spreads is hard to achieve without an underlying structure
Show awareness that breaking the grid occasionally is a deliberate choice, not the absence of one
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A grid isn't there to restrict creativity, it's there so a reader's eye already knows roughly where to look before they've even read a word, which matters hugely across a sixty page magazine rather than a single poster. I used a strict column grid on a school newsletter I redesigned last year and readership feedback actually improved because people could scan it faster. That said, I think the most interesting layouts are the ones where the designer clearly knows the grid well enough to break it on purpose, for one image or headline that needs to breathe.

commonMistakes: Treating grids as purely a technical rule with no connection to how readers actually process a page
Claiming free form layout is always more creative or more skilled
Not recognizing that breaking a grid intentionally is different from never having one
followUps: Can you think of a design where breaking the grid actually helped communication rather than hurting it?

question: How do you decide whether two typefaces actually work well together in the same layout?
lookingFor: Practical criteria for pairing type beyond 'it looks nice', showing genuine hands-on experimentation.

bullets: Look for enough contrast in structure, such as a serif with a sans serif, rather than two fonts that are too similar
Check that both typefaces share a similar mood or era so they don't fight each other
Test the pairing at actual sizes and weights used in the layout, not just side by side in isolation
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I usually start by picking one typeface to carry the personality of the piece and a second, quieter one to do the heavy lifting for body text, because two loud fonts in the same layout tend to compete rather than cooperate. I also check that they're different enough structurally, so I'll pair a geometric sans with a humanist serif rather than two sans serifs that just look like a mistake. The real test for me is setting actual paragraph text and headlines together at real size, because pairings that look fine as two words on a mood board sometimes fall apart once there's a whole page of content.

commonMistakes: Choosing fonts purely because they're personal favorites with no structural reasoning
Picking two typefaces that are almost identical, creating a look that reads as a mistake
Never testing the pairing at real sizes and with real content
followUps: What's a typeface pairing you've used in your own work, and why did you pick it?

question: Walk us through how you'd establish visual hierarchy on a poster that has five different pieces of information all competing for attention.
lookingFor: A structured approach to ranking information by importance and using scale, weight, color, and position to guide the eye.

bullets: Start by ranking the five elements by what the audience genuinely needs to see first, second, and so on
Use size, weight, contrast, and placement, not just size alone, to separate levels of the hierarchy
Explain that not everything can be emphasized, since making everything loud makes nothing stand out
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: The first thing I'd do before touching any type is actually rank the five pieces of information myself, because the client will often say everything is equally important and it usually isn't. Once I know the priority, I use scale for the headline, then I drop weight and size down through a clear sequence, and I'll use color sparingly, maybe just one accent, so it doesn't dilute itself. I learned the hard way on an event poster I made in school that if you try to make every line bold and bright, the whole thing goes flat and nothing actually reads first.

commonMistakes: Making everything large or bold because it all feels important
Relying only on size to create hierarchy and ignoring weight, spacing, or color
Not asking what the audience actually needs to read first
followUps: What would you cut entirely if the client refused to let you prioritize?

question: Can you explain the difference between kerning, tracking, and leading?
lookingFor: Clear, correct definitions of core typographic terms, showing hands-on familiarity rather than textbook memorization.

bullets: Kerning is the space between two specific letters, adjusted individually
Tracking is the uniform spacing applied across a whole word or block of text
Leading is the vertical space between lines of text
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Kerning is adjusting the space between two individual letters, like tightening the gap between a capital A and V because they naturally leave an awkward hole between them. Tracking is different because it adjusts the spacing evenly across an entire word or paragraph, which I'll often open up slightly on a headline set in all capitals so it doesn't feel cramped. Leading is the vertical space between lines, and getting that right is honestly what separates readable body text from a block that feels exhausting to get through, even if the typeface itself is a good choice.

commonMistakes: Confusing kerning with tracking, treating them as the same thing
Forgetting leading affects readability as much as the typeface choice does
Giving a definition with no practical example of when you'd adjust each
followUps: When would you deliberately use tight tracking on a headline?

question: What do you think the Bauhaus movement got right, and where do you think its principles fall short in design today?
lookingFor: Genuine engagement with design history and the ability to critically evaluate a movement rather than just admire it.

bullets: Identify what Bauhaus contributed, such as form following function and unifying craft with industrial production
Offer an honest critique, such as its principles sometimes producing cold or impersonal results
Connect the discussion to how those ideas still show up, or get pushed back against, in current design work
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think Bauhaus was right that a design should earn every element it uses, that form should come from function rather than decoration for its own sake, and that idea still underpins a lot of good UI and product design today. Where I think it falls short is that taken too literally, it can produce work that feels sterile or one size fits all, when actually different audiences and cultures respond to warmth and ornament in ways strict functionalism dismissed. I find it interesting that a lot of the maximalist branding coming back into fashion now almost feels like a direct reaction against that legacy.

commonMistakes: Reciting Bauhaus history with no personal opinion or critique
Dismissing the movement entirely without acknowledging its real influence
Confusing Bauhaus with a different, unrelated movement
followUps: Can you name a piece of design today that you think is directly influenced by Bauhaus thinking?

question: How would a designer use visual metaphor to communicate an abstract idea, like trust or growth, without using any words?
lookingFor: Understanding of how shape, color, and symbol carry meaning, and awareness that meaning is culturally learned, not universal.

bullets: Give a concrete example of a visual device, such as an upward arrow or interlocking shapes, mapped to an abstract concept
Acknowledge that visual metaphors rely on shared cultural understanding rather than being universally obvious
Show awareness that overused metaphors, like a handshake for trust, can feel cliche
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: For something like growth, I might reach for an upward or expanding form, a sprouting shape, or a sequence of elements that increase in size, because our eyes are already trained to read that direction as progress. But I try to be careful, because a lot of these visual shortcuts, like a handshake meaning trust or a lightbulb meaning an idea, are so overused that they stop actually saying anything fresh. What I find more interesting is finding a metaphor rooted in the specific brand or story, rather than a generic symbol, because that's what actually makes a mark memorable instead of interchangeable.

commonMistakes: Assuming all visual symbols are universally understood across cultures
Relying on the most cliche symbol available instead of a fresher metaphor
Describing the concept only in words with no actual visual example
followUps: Can you think of a logo that uses visual metaphor particularly well?

subtopic: Negative space as a communicative tool
question: Talk us through how negative space can do as much communicative work in a design as the positive shapes do.
lookingFor: Practical understanding that empty space is an active design element, not leftover area.

bullets: Give a concrete example, like a logo where the negative space forms a second image or meaning
Explain that negative space also controls pacing and breathing room in a layout
Show that empty space is a deliberate decision, not simply unused area
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: The classic example everyone brings up is the FedEx logo with the arrow hidden between the E and the X, and it's a good one because it shows negative space isn't just what's left over, it can actually carry a second layer of meaning entirely. Beyond logos, I think about negative space in layout too, like giving a product shot room to breathe on a poster rather than cramming text right up against it, because that empty space is what makes the one thing you do include feel important. I try to treat white space as an actual design decision I'm making, not the parts of the page I just haven't filled in yet.

commonMistakes: Treating negative space as wasted or unused area rather than an active choice
Only mentioning the FedEx example with no personal understanding beyond it
Cramming a layout full because empty space feels like a missed opportunity
followUps: Have you ever removed something from your own work to give it more breathing room?

question: Generative AI tools can now produce a full logo concept or mood board in seconds. What do you think that means for what a graphic design degree should actually teach?
lookingFor: A thoughtful, non-defensive take on AI's role that distinguishes execution speed from the judgment and taste a designer brings.

bullets: Acknowledge honestly what AI tools are actually good at, like fast exploration or generating raw options
Argue for what remains distinctly human, such as understanding a brief, taste, and knowing which idea actually solves the problem
Avoid both extremes, neither dismissing AI entirely nor treating it as a replacement for design judgment
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I don't think AI replaces the part of design that actually matters, which is understanding a client's real problem and having the taste to know which of a hundred possible directions is the right one, but I'd be lying if I said it hasn't changed how fast I can explore ideas. I use it sometimes to generate quick visual references when I'm stuck, the same way I'd flip through a book of old posters, but I still do the actual thinking and refining by hand because the output on its own is rarely specific enough to a real brief. I think a good course now needs to teach critical judgment and editing even more than it teaches raw execution, because execution is getting faster for everyone.

commonMistakes: Dismissing AI entirely as irrelevant to real design work
Suggesting AI can fully replace the design process with no pushback
Giving a vague, rehearsed answer with no personal experience using the tools
followUps: Have you used an AI tool in your own design work, and how did you decide where to draw the line?

question: A client asks you to design packaging that makes a product look noticeably larger than what's actually inside the box. What do you do?
lookingFor: Ethical reasoning that balances client relationships with honesty toward consumers, arriving at a workable middle ground rather than a snap answer.

bullets: Recognize the tension between the client's request and misleading the end consumer
Suggest raising the concern directly with the client rather than either refusing outright or silently complying
Offer a constructive alternative, such as legal net weight labeling or a design that's honest but still appealing
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: My instinct would be that making a package deliberately look bigger than the product inside crosses into misleading the person actually buying it, and I don't think I'd want my name on that even if the client is happy. I wouldn't just refuse and walk away though, I'd explain my concern directly and try to find a version that's still visually strong and shelf ready without the exaggeration, maybe by focusing on better photography or a bolder layout instead of empty space inside the box. If the client insisted on something I genuinely thought was deceptive to the consumer, I think I'd have to be honest that I'm not comfortable designing it.

commonMistakes: Complying immediately with no ethical consideration because the client is paying
Refusing outright with no attempt to find a workable alternative
Ignoring that consumers, not just the client, are affected by the decision
followUps: Would your answer change if the exaggeration were common practice across the whole industry?

question: You're asked to design branding that uses a cultural symbol that isn't part of your own heritage. How would you approach that responsibly?
lookingFor: Awareness of cultural sensitivity and appropriation, balanced against an openness to cross-cultural design done with genuine research and respect.

bullets: Show awareness of the difference between respectful engagement and appropriation without understanding
Propose concrete steps, such as researching the symbol's meaning and, ideally, consulting people from that culture
Avoid both extremes, refusing to engage with any culture outside your own, or using symbols carelessly
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd want to actually understand what the symbol means and where it comes from before I put it anywhere near a design, rather than just using it because it looks visually interesting, because that's usually where appropriation happens, when a symbol gets flattened into decoration and stripped of its actual meaning. If it's possible, I'd try to get input from someone connected to that culture, even informally, because there's a real difference between how something reads from inside a culture and how it might land from outside it. I think designers can absolutely draw from cultures beyond their own, but it has to come with real research and humility, not just visual borrowing.

commonMistakes: Treating cultural symbols as purely decorative with no research into their meaning
Refusing to engage with any culture outside your own as the only safe option
Not recognizing the difference between respectful reference and appropriation
followUps: Can you think of a real example of branding that got this wrong?

question: Where do you personally draw the line between being inspired by another designer's work and actually copying it?
lookingFor: A clear, defensible personal standard distinguishing genuine influence from derivative copying.

bullets: Distinguish between absorbing a technique or principle versus lifting a specific composition or solution
Mention that being inspired should lead to your own interpretation shaped by your own brief and context
Show self-awareness by referencing how they've handled this in their own work
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: For me the line is whether I'm taking away a principle, like how a designer used color to create depth, or whether I'm lifting the actual specific solution and just changing a few details, because the first teaches me something and the second is just copying with extra steps. When I was working on my art foundation project I looked closely at a poster series I admired for how it used cropping, but I made myself sketch completely different compositions from scratch rather than referencing the image directly while I worked. I think a good test is whether someone who knew the reference well could still recognize your piece as clearly your own solution to a different brief.

commonMistakes: Claiming influence is never a problem as long as you admire the work
Being unable to articulate any personal standard at all
Not acknowledging that copying can happen unintentionally through overreliance on references
followUps: Has a piece of your own work ever ended up too close to a reference, and how did you catch it?

question: Imagine you designed a new logo for a well loved brand and the public backlash online is instant and fierce. What would you actually do in the first forty eight hours?
lookingFor: Composure under criticism, ability to separate genuine feedback from noise, and a professional rather than defensive response.

bullets: Avoid panicking or immediately reversing the decision without understanding the actual feedback
Distinguish between substantive criticism and reflexive resistance to any change
Describe working with the client or team on a considered response, not a solo public reaction
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Honestly, my first move wouldn't be to defend the work publicly, it would be to actually read through the criticism carefully and separate the parts that are just people resisting any change from the parts that might be pointing at a genuine problem with the design. Brands get backlash almost every time they change a logo people are attached to, so I wouldn't assume the work failed just because it's loud online, but I also wouldn't dismiss it out of pride. I'd want to sit down with the client and figure out together whether this settles down once people adjust, or whether there's something in the feedback worth actually revisiting.

commonMistakes: Assuming all backlash means the design failed and it should be scrapped immediately
Dismissing all criticism as people simply resisting change
Reacting emotionally or defensively instead of professionally
followUps: How would you tell the difference between backlash that fades and backlash pointing at a real flaw?

question: Why do you think accessible design, things like color contrast standards and legible type sizes, has become such a bigger part of graphic design briefs in recent years?
lookingFor: Awareness of accessibility as both an ethical and practical shift in the field, not just a compliance checkbox.

bullets: Mention growing awareness that a meaningful share of any audience has some visual or cognitive difference
Note legal and platform driven pressure, such as WCAG standards, pushing accessibility into mainstream briefs
Argue that accessible design usually makes work clearer for everyone, not just a smaller group
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think it's partly that the industry has finally caught up to the fact that a real chunk of any audience has some kind of visual difference, whether that's color blindness or low vision, and designing as if everyone sees a screen the same way was always a flawed assumption. There's also more legal and platform pressure now, with standards like WCAG actually built into a lot of client briefs rather than being an afterthought. What I find genuinely interesting is that most accessibility fixes, like stronger contrast or clearer type hierarchy, tend to make a design better for everyone, not just the audience it was specifically written for.

commonMistakes: Treating accessibility as a purely legal or box-ticking requirement
Framing accessible design as a constraint that limits creativity
Showing no awareness of any actual accessibility standard or guideline
followUps: Can you think of a design choice that improves accessibility and also improves the design overall?

question: What actually changes about your design process when you're designing for print compared to designing for a screen?
lookingFor: Practical understanding of the technical and experiential differences between the two mediums.

bullets: Mention technical differences such as color mode, CMYK versus RGB, resolution, and bleed
Note that screen design has to account for varying sizes, interaction, and motion in a way print doesn't
Discuss that print is a fixed final object while digital work is often iterative and can be updated
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: The most obvious shift for me is color and resolution, working in CMYK and thinking about bleed and paper stock for print, versus RGB and thinking about how a design holds up on a five inch phone screen and a large monitor at once for digital. But the bigger mental shift is that print is final the moment it's printed, so I check everything obsessively before it goes to press, while digital work is something I can actually watch people use and adjust afterward. I also think about pacing differently, a print piece is read in one physical moment, but a screen design has to account for scrolling, interaction, and sometimes motion, which changes how I build hierarchy.

commonMistakes: Only mentioning color mode with no discussion of interaction or format differences
Treating print and digital as interchangeable with no adjustment to process
Ignoring that digital designs can be updated after launch while print cannot
followUps: Which medium do you personally find more challenging to design for, and why?

subtopic: Responding to critique of your best work
question: A tutor tells you the piece you consider the strongest in your portfolio is actually the weakest. How would you respond to that in the moment?
lookingFor: Openness to critique without defensiveness, paired with the confidence to ask genuine follow-up questions.

bullets: Show a first instinct of listening and asking for specifics rather than immediately defending the work
Acknowledge that a designer's own attachment to a piece can distort how objectively they see it
Describe how they'd actually use that feedback, not just accept it politely
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: My first reaction probably would sting a little, because that piece usually means something to you personally, but I'd try to actually ask what specifically isn't working rather than just defending it on instinct. I think designers, myself included, often love a piece because of what it took to make it, the late nights or the personal meaning behind it, and that's not the same as it actually being the strongest piece to an outside eye. I'd rather understand the critique properly and either revise the piece or swap it out than protect my own attachment to it just because I like it.

commonMistakes: Getting defensive and arguing against the critique instead of listening
Agreeing immediately with no real reflection, just to avoid conflict
Failing to distinguish personal attachment from actual design quality
followUps: Has that actually happened to you with a piece of your own work?

question: There's been a visible swing back toward busy, maximalist branding recently after years of clean minimalism. What do you make of that trend?
lookingFor: Awareness of current visual trends and an ability to reason about why design fashions shift rather than just naming the trend.

bullets: Show awareness of the trend itself with a specific example, not just a vague reference
Offer a reason for the shift, such as brands wanting to feel distinct after minimalism became generic
Give a personal opinion on when maximalism works and when restraint still wins
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think it happened partly because minimalism became so widespread that a lot of brands ended up looking almost identical, that same clean sans serif logo everyone jokes about online, and maximalism is one way brands are trying to feel distinct and human again. I actually like a lot of the recent maximalist branding when it's done with real intention, layered pattern and color that still has a clear hierarchy underneath it, but I think it fails when it's just busy for the sake of standing out with nothing organizing it. My honest opinion is that neither approach is inherently better, it depends on whether the chaos or the restraint actually serves what the brand needs to say.

commonMistakes: Treating one style as objectively superior with no situational reasoning
Naming the trend with no specific example or personal opinion
Confusing maximalism with simply cluttered or unplanned design
followUps: Can you name a brand you think handled a maximalist redesign well?

question: You're asked to design an anti-smoking campaign aimed at teenagers. Fear-based imagery is proven to grab attention but is also criticized as manipulative. Would you use it?
lookingFor: Ethical reasoning that weighs effectiveness against manipulation, landing on a considered position rather than a reflexive yes or no.

bullets: Acknowledge the genuine tension between what's effective and what feels manipulative
Distinguish between fear used to inform honestly and fear used purely to shock without substance
Reach a considered position, likely favoring honest, evidence-based fear over exploitative shock
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I don't think fear based imagery is automatically wrong, because if the underlying facts are true and the goal is genuinely to protect teenagers, showing real consequences isn't manipulation, it's honesty that happens to be uncomfortable. Where I'd draw the line is if the imagery exaggerates or distorts reality purely to shock, because at that point it's not informing anyone, it's just using fear as a trick, and I think teenagers can usually tell the difference and tune it out anyway. If I were designing that campaign, I'd want the fear to come from something true and specific rather than generic horror, because I think that's both more ethical and honestly more effective.

commonMistakes: Giving a flat yes or no with no reasoning about manipulation versus honesty
Assuming fear based messaging is always either fully ethical or fully wrong
Ignoring the target audience's ability to see through exaggerated messaging
followUps: How would you test whether a piece of imagery has crossed from honest to manipulative?

question: How do environmental concerns, like paper stock and ink, actually factor into decisions a graphic designer makes on a print project?
lookingFor: Practical awareness of sustainable print practices, not just a vague statement about caring about the environment.

bullets: Mention concrete choices, such as recycled or FSC certified paper stock and vegetable based inks
Note that print run size and finishing choices, like foil or lamination, also affect environmental impact
Show awareness that sustainability decisions sometimes involve a trade-off with cost or visual effect
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: It comes down to real, specific choices, like specifying recycled or FSC certified stock instead of virgin paper, or pushing for soy or vegetable based inks over standard petroleum ones, which are decisions I actually have to research and recommend rather than assume the printer will handle. Finishing matters too, things like foil stamping or plastic lamination look great but are much harder to recycle, so sometimes the more sustainable choice means giving something up visually. I try to be upfront with a client that sustainable choices sometimes cost slightly more or look a little different, and let them make an informed decision rather than deciding quietly on their behalf.

commonMistakes: Giving a vague statement about caring for the environment with no concrete practices
Ignoring that sustainable choices can involve real trade-offs in cost or finish
Assuming sustainability is entirely the printer's responsibility, not the designer's
followUps: Have you made a design decision on a real project specifically for environmental reasons?

question: When, if ever, is it acceptable for a typeface choice to sacrifice legibility for the sake of expressive impact?
lookingFor: Nuanced reasoning about context-dependent trade-offs between readability and expression, rather than a blanket rule.

bullets: Distinguish between contexts where legibility is essential, like body text or safety information, and contexts where impact matters more, like a single headline or album cover
Explain that even expressive type needs a floor of readability appropriate to its context and audience
Give a concrete example of expressive type used well despite reduced legibility
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think it depends entirely on how much reading the piece is actually asking of someone, a warning label or a paragraph of body text has to prioritize legibility because the whole point is communication at speed, but a gig poster or an album title has room to sacrifice some legibility for mood, because the audience is willing to spend a second longer decoding it as part of the experience. Even then I don't think legibility should disappear completely, there's a difference between type that's stylized and type that's genuinely unreadable, and the best expressive typography I've seen still respects the audience enough to be decoded with a little effort. My rule of thumb is that the stakes of the message should decide how much legibility I'm willing to trade.

commonMistakes: Treating legibility as either always essential or never important, with no context
Failing to give a specific example distinguishing when each approach applies
Confusing expressive type with type that's simply poorly executed
followUps: Can you show or describe a piece of expressive typography you think gets that balance right?

question: How would you balance staying within a brand's strict style guide against wanting to push a genuinely new creative idea?
lookingFor: Understanding that constraints and creativity aren't opposites, plus a sensible process for proposing change within a system.

bullets: Show respect for why brand guidelines exist, namely consistency and recognition over time
Explain that a strong idea can usually be tested within the existing system before proposing to break it
Describe a constructive way to propose genuine change, rather than ignoring the guidelines outright
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I actually think constraints tend to make me more creative, not less, because a strict style guide forces me to find the idea inside the system rather than reaching for whatever's easiest outside it. If I genuinely think an idea needs to break the guidelines, I'd first try to prove it works within them, and only if it still feels compromised would I bring the idea to whoever owns the brand as a proposed evolution, with a clear case for why it's worth the risk. I don't think ignoring a style guide because you personally find it limiting is good practice, brand consistency exists for a reason, but guides can and should evolve if there's a strong enough case.

commonMistakes: Treating brand guidelines as purely restrictive with no understanding of their purpose
Suggesting they'd ignore the guidelines whenever they personally disagreed
No process offered for how a genuine new idea would actually get proposed
followUps: Have you worked within a strict brief before, and how did you find room to be creative inside it?

question: How did you decide which pieces to include in your portfolio, and which ones to leave out?
lookingFor: Evidence of self-editing judgment and the ability to curate rather than simply display everything made.

bullets: Explain a clear criteria used, such as range of skills shown or strength of final execution
Mention a piece deliberately left out and why, showing real self-editing
Connect the selection to what they want it to say about them as a developing designer
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I tried to pick pieces that each showed a different muscle, so there's a branding project, something typography heavy, and one piece that's more illustrative, rather than five variations on the same skill. I actually left out a poster series I spent a long time on, because looking at it honestly, the concept was weaker than the execution, and I didn't want a portfolio full of technically polished work with nothing underneath it. I wanted the whole set to say I can think through a concept properly, not just that I'm competent with software, so anything that leaned too heavily on the second thing without the first got cut.

commonMistakes: Including every piece ever made with no real curation or reasoning
Choosing pieces based only on technical polish with no conceptual strength
Unable to name anything they deliberately excluded
followUps: What's the weakest piece still in your portfolio, and why did you keep it in?

question: Is it lazy design to build a project around stock photography, or do you think that's an unfair judgment?
lookingFor: A balanced, non-dogmatic view that separates skillful use of stock imagery from lazy reliance on it.

bullets: Reject the blanket claim that all stock photography use is lazy
Distinguish between thoughtful selection and treatment of stock images versus generic, unedited use
Note practical realities, like budget or timeline, that make stock imagery a legitimate tool
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think calling stock photography lazy by default is unfair, because plenty of great designers use it skillfully, cropping, color grading, and combining images in ways that feel completely custom even though the source wasn't originally shot for the project. What actually reads as lazy to me is dropping in an obviously generic stock photo with no treatment at all, the kind where you can tell it's the same image showing up on three other websites. Budget and timeline are real constraints too, not every project can afford original photography, and I think the skill is in how thoughtfully you select and adapt the image, not whether you commissioned it yourself.

commonMistakes: Dismissing all stock photography use as inherently lazy or low quality
Defending stock imagery use with no acknowledgment of when it does look generic
Ignoring the practical budget realities that make stock photography common
followUps: Can you think of a project where stock imagery was used really well?

question: Pick a logo you think is badly designed and walk us through what's actually wrong with it.
lookingFor: The ability to critique with specific, technical reasoning rather than vague personal taste.

bullets: Name a specific real logo, not a hypothetical or overly safe example
Give concrete design reasons, such as poor scalability, weak contrast, or unclear concept
Avoid pure taste judgments and root the critique in function and communication
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I've never liked the Pepsi logo redesign from a few years back, the one with the smile shape and the wavy divider, mostly because the concept behind it, described in that leaked strategy document about cosmic energy fields, doesn't actually read at all when you just look at the mark itself. Functionally it also loses clarity at small sizes, the subtle curve in the divider barely survives being shrunk down onto a can, so it's not just a taste issue for me, it's that the idea and the execution don't hold together under real use. I think a strong logo critique should always separate whether something is unfamiliar from whether it's actually failing to do its job, and for me this one is the second thing.

commonMistakes: Giving a critique based purely on personal taste with no functional reasoning
Choosing an overly safe or obvious example with no real analysis
Being needlessly harsh with no constructive understanding of the constraints involved
followUps: How would you redesign it if you were given the brief today?

question: You've been given a strong concept, but the client's budget only covers black and white printing and no photography. How would you make the concept still work?
lookingFor: Creative problem-solving under real constraints, showing that limitation can sharpen rather than kill a concept.

bullets: Reframe the constraint as a creative direction rather than treating it purely as a limitation
Suggest concrete alternatives, such as illustration, strong typography, texture, or pattern instead of photography
Show that they'd protect the core concept even as the execution changes
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: My first move would be to figure out whether black and white and no photography actually kills the concept, or whether it just means I need a different way to say the same thing, because most strong ideas don't live in the color palette or the photograph, they live in the underlying thought. I'd probably lean into typography and pattern instead, maybe strong illustration or a clever use of tone and texture within black and white, since limitation like that has pushed me to more interesting solutions before, not less interesting ones. I'd rather protect the actual idea and change how it's executed than water down the concept just to force in a full color photographic layout that was never within budget anyway.

commonMistakes: Treating the constraint as something that simply ruins the original concept
Offering no concrete alternative techniques, just vague reassurance
Abandoning the core concept entirely instead of adapting its execution
followUps: Can you think of a real design you admire that works specifically because of a similar constraint?

subtopic: Designing within a system versus bespoke work
question: How do you think about designing within a reusable design system or component library, compared to creating something bespoke each time?
lookingFor: Awareness of how design systems have changed graphic and digital design practice, with a balanced view of their trade-offs.

bullets: Explain what a design system offers, such as consistency, speed, and scalability across many products or pages
Acknowledge the trade-off, that systems can constrain individual creative expression on any single piece
Show an understanding of when bespoke work is still worth the extra time and cost
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A design system is really about consistency at scale, so that a hundred different screens or documents all feel like they came from the same place even if a dozen different people worked on them, and I think that's genuinely valuable, not just corporate box ticking. The trade-off is that it can flatten the more expressive, one-off decisions that make a single piece memorable, since you're working inside a set of predefined components rather than inventing a new solution each time. I think the two aren't actually opposites though, the best systems I've seen still leave room for a bespoke moment, a hero piece or a launch campaign, where the brand gets to step outside the system briefly and then return to it.

commonMistakes: Treating design systems as purely restrictive with no understanding of their purpose
Assuming bespoke work is always better with no acknowledgment of scale problems
Showing no awareness that design systems have become central to modern digital work
followUps: Have you ever worked with any kind of component library or style guide yourself?
